Which Metro offices deal with a Davidson County tax bill?

Two Metro Nashville offices split the work. The Assessor of Property appraises and classifies every parcel. The Office of the Metropolitan Trustee mails statements and collects payment. Assessment amounts are not its decision.

Each September the Trustee receives the certified roll from the Assessor. Visit the Trustee in the Howard Office Building, 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 220, any weekday between 8 in the morning and 4:30 in the afternoon. For value questions, call the Assessor at 615-862-6080.

Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville are the only cities in the county that bill separate city taxes. Their numbers are 615-297-6041, 615-859-0596 and 615-851-2200. Every other city address pays through the Metropolitan Trustee.

Payment calendar and interest

Statements go into the mail during the first week of October. You can start paying on the first Monday of October. To avoid interest, the whole amount must arrive by the last day of February, and installments along the way are allowed.

After the cutoff, interest of 1.5% (18% a year) is added to the base tax on the first of every month, beginning March 1. The Trustee's collections division works delinquent accounts from March through the following February, and after that the Clerk and Master's office takes over collection.

How payments reach the Metropolitan Trustee

You can pay on the Trustee's website, by mail, or at the counter in the Howard Office Building. Payments sent through your own bank's bill pay count on the day the Trustee receives them.

  • Make checks payable to Metropolitan Trustee, PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.
  • Cards cost 2.35% of the payment, with a $2.00 floor, and an E-Check costs $1.00. Metro keeps none of it.
  • A postmark sets the payment date for mail, but a private meter stamp does not. With no postmark, the day the envelope arrives counts.
  • A website payment is credited on the day you make it.

New owners should read the closing statement or ask the title company who owes the tax, since unpaid taxes continue to accrue against the property.

The 2025 reappraisal and rates

The final countywide median value increase was 45% as of January 1, 2025, four years after the previous reappraisal in 2021. Owners were given more time than usual to appeal.

State law requires a Certified Tax Rate after each reappraisal so local governments do not collect a windfall on existing property. The 2025 rates came to $2.782 per $100 in the General Services District and $2.814 per $100 in the Urban Services District, down from $2.922 and $3.254 in 2024.

The Urban Services District pays for garbage pickup, street lights and sidewalks that owners in the General Services District arrange on their own.

How do you work out a Davidson County bill?

Multiply the appraised value by the 25% residential ratio, then apply the rate for your district per $100 of the result.

Your notice has a Tax Jurisdiction box that says whether you are in the GSD, the USD or one of the satellite cities. Those are Ridgetop, Goodlettsville, Belle Meade, Berry Hill, Forest Hills and Oak Hill, and their owners pay the GSD rate plus the city's own rate. Downtown properties may also sit inside the Central Business Improvement District or the Gulch Business Improvement District, which add their own assessments.

How to contest a Davidson County value

The Assessor handles an informal review first. A formal appeal then goes before an independent hearing officer or the Metropolitan Board of Equalization, scheduled through the Assessor's call center at 615-862-6059. Call that number for the current year's request and filing dates.

Owners who miss the formal deadline may lose the right to appeal for that tax year, so do not wait on it.

During an appeal, pay at least the undisputed share before delinquency, along with any past-due prior-year tax. To find the undisputed portion, divide the value you claim by the Assessor's value and multiply by the tax due. When the final certificate of assessment issues, you either receive a refund or owe the balance plus interest at the Federal Reserve composite prime rate minus two points.

Tax relief and the tax freeze

Low-income elderly or disabled homeowners and disabled veteran owners can have local taxes reimbursed by the state, and owners 65 and older can join the Trustee's tax freeze. What you qualify for depends on age or disability, ownership and residency, and income.

  • Elderly and disabled relief: applicants must turn 65 by December 31 of the tax year or be disabled by that date, and must document ownership with a bill, deed or probated will.
  • Disabled veteran owners: a 100% disability rating is required, there is no income limit, and relief covers the first $175,000 of market value.
  • Tax freeze: owners 65 and older who live in the home can freeze the bill at the amount for the year they qualify. Applications are due by April 5 each year, and the Trustee's number is 615-862-6330.

Ask the Trustee for the current income limits before you apply.

Nashville-Davidson housing in brief

Davidson County is governed as Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson County. The July 2025 estimate is 745,904 residents, up 4.2% from April 2020. Survey results for 2020 to 2024 put the middle owner-occupied home value at $417,400 and typical gross rent at $1,582. Owners live in 52.8% of homes, which leaves renters near half of households, so a seller may have a tenant in place.

What happens to a delinquent parcel?

Delinquent parcels can end up at a tax sale auction run through Chancery Court. Auctions are held one Wednesday a month starting in June, and sales are final, but the owner has a one-year right to redeem the property. The buyer earns 10% annual interest on the purchase price during the redemption period.

The county does not help purchasers with any foreclosure or eviction. Anyone running behind should phone the Trustee's collections division before March 1 for a payoff figure, and a seller should hand that number to the title company.

Frequently asked questions

When is Davidson County property tax due?

Metro mails statements in the opening week of October and takes payments beginning the first Monday of that month. Pay everything by the last day of February and no interest applies. From March 1, interest of 1.5% is added each month.

What is the Davidson County property tax rate?

For 2025 the General Services District rate is $2.782 per $100 of assessed value and the Urban Services District rate is $2.814. Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville bill separate city taxes on top of the GSD rate.

How much did Davidson County values rise in the 2025 reappraisal?

The final countywide median increase was 45% as of January 1, 2025. Council district medians ranged from 38% to 54%. The Certified Tax Rate was then set to keep revenue on existing property level.

Does Davidson County accept partial property tax payments?

Yes, installments are fine during the collection period, though interest still applies unless the whole balance is in by the last day of February. A card adds 2.35% with a $2.00 minimum, and an E-Check adds $1.00.

Who pays the property tax when a Davidson County house is sold?

Look at the closing statement. The answer turns on the transfer date, and because unpaid taxes keep accruing against the property, have the title company confirm who owes what.

Offices that handle Knox County property tax

Two county offices share this job, and both sit inside the Knoxville City-County Building at 400 Main Street. Values and appeals belong to the Property Assessor at 865-215-2360. Payments belong to the Trustee in Suite 427 at 865-215-2305. Both open at eight and close at half past four on weekdays. A separate Assessor line, 865-215-2362, covers business personal property.

The Trustee's payment page lists six places to pay in person. Remote options:

  • Online, through the county's lookup tool; cards add a 2.5% fee and e-checks add $1.00
  • Phone: 865-215-2305, then option 3
  • Mail: P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901

The Trustee's office also takes address changes online. The Assessor takes mailing address changes by phone at 865-215-2360.

Tax rate and how it is split

The fiscal 2026 levy is $1.5540 for each $100 of assessed value, and the County Commission sets it alongside the budget. Homes are assessed at 25% of appraised value, commercial property at 40%, and business personal property at 30%. The Assessor's FAQ gives the formula: appraised value, times the assessment percentage, times the combined city and county rate.

Living inside Knoxville means the city rate is added to the county one. The city's rate comes from the City of Knoxville, so call there for today's number.

Tax calendar

The Assessor's calendar page lays out the tax year. Taxes for the current year come due on October 1. Pay by February 28 and there is no penalty or interest. A prior year's bill is delinquent from March 1.

The assessment side keeps its own schedule:

  • January 1 fixes ownership and condition for assessment purposes
  • March 15 is the last day to apply for greenbelt
  • May 20 is the exemption application cutoff, and change notices should be in the mail by then
  • June 1 opens the County Board of Equalization, which sits through the month
  • August 1 is the usual last day to reach the State Board, or 45 days after the county board's notice when that is later

Reappraisal here takes two years. The first is field work and sales data. The second applies the valuation models and mails new values along with appeal instructions. A higher value does not guarantee a higher bill, since the Commission may lower the rate afterward. Use the Assessor's calculator and parcel lookup to see where a value stands before the notice reaches you.

Tax relief and the senior freeze

Relief runs through the Trustee. For the 2026 senior freeze, an owner must turn 65 by December 31, 2026, and combined 2025 income for the owner, spouse and every deed owner must stay under $63,470, with VA income counted. Separate state relief reaches disabled-veteran owners, up to $444 for 2026 with no income limit, and the widows and widowers of a disabled veteran who have not remarried.

Applying early matters for a seller. If your relief credit is still pending when you list, tell the closing agent so the payoff and any credit are handled correctly at the table.

Think of relief as a state-funded credit toward payment instead of an exemption, so the bill still arrives and has to be paid. Enrollment for the 2026 tax year opens October 1, 2026 and closes April 5, 2027. The state fixes those dates, so the county cannot move them or grant extensions. Email applications are not accepted. You can request a form at taxrelief@knoxcounty.org or call the recorded information line at 865-215-8554.

Knox County market snapshot

The county counted 511,453 people on July 1, 2025, a 6.8% gain over April 2020. Owners occupy roughly 65.2% of homes, with a median value of $320,900. Median household income is $74,222. Typical monthly cost for an owner with a mortgage is $1,589, and typical rent is $1,261. Home values this high make an accurate assessment worth checking.

Knoxville is the county seat, and Farragut is in the county too. One Assessor and one Trustee serve all of it, so a Knoxville homeowner and a rural owner call the same numbers.

What this means when you sell: the tax bill follows the property, not the person, and the January 1 owner is on the roll. Before an offer is accepted, look up your parcel on the county lookup, see whether the current year is paid, and check whether earlier years show a balance. A clean record makes the title company's job simple, and a balance simply gets added to the payoff list. Call the Trustee at 865-215-2305 if the lookup shows something you do not recognize.

Selling a Knox County house with tax owed

Any change of ownership, even a private sale or a move into a trust or estate, prompts a sales questionnaire from the Assessor. The owner's name changes after the new deed is recorded with the Register of Deeds, a step that may take a week. Still seeing the old name a month later? Call 865-215-2360. The closing agent will get a payoff from the Trustee covering this year's bill plus any delinquent years.

Under Tennessee Code section 67-5-603, mid-year changes are prorated. A fire, a demolition or a completed addition between January 1 and September 1 alters the assessed value for just part of that year. Rebuilt or demolished something? Ask for a field review so the bill reflects the house you are actually selling. Ask the Assessor at 865-215-2360 how long the review will take before you set a closing date. Buyers' agents often pull the assessment history, so a record that matches the real house avoids questions late in the deal.

Years of nonpayment can lead to a tax sale handled through the Clerk and Master, where bidders must be current on their own taxes. The Trustee announces a sale date once the court sets one. An owner with delinquent years can have the balance paid from sale proceeds at closing, and a cash sale on a short timeline often suits an owner who is behind.

Gather these before you list: your latest tax notice, the parcel number, any exemption or relief paperwork, and a note of repairs or demolitions since January 1. The closing agent needs the first two, and the last two keep the bill accurate.

Frequently asked questions

When are Knox County property taxes due?

Pay by February 28 to avoid penalty and interest. Current-year taxes come due October 1, and a prior year's bill turns delinquent March 1.

What is the Knox County property tax rate?

For fiscal 2026 the county levies $1.5540 per $100 of assessed value. If you live inside a city, add that city's rate, which you can get from the city.

Where does a Knox County owner file an assessment appeal?

The county board comes first and starts meeting June 1. After that, the state board takes cases filed by August 1 or 45 days after the county notice went out. The Assessor at 865-215-2360 can arrange a field review before either step.

What is the deadline for the Knox County senior tax freeze?

The cutoff is April 5, 2027 for the 2026 tax year. You must reach age 65 by December 31, 2026, and 2025 combined income has to be under $63,470.

Can I sell a Knox County house that owes property tax?

Yes. The Trustee gives a payoff figure and the closing agent takes it out of the seller's proceeds. Years of nonpayment can send an account to a court-run tax sale.

Who sends and collects the bill

Three offices handle county tax here, and Memphis adds a second bill. The Assessor of Property puts a value on each parcel. The County Commission picks the county rate. The Trustee multiplies that rate against every $100 of assessed value and mails the notice to the address on the Assessor's records. A lender that escrows your taxes can look up the details and pay for you, so the notice may only be a file copy.

  • Trustee: 157 Poplar Avenue, 2nd Floor, Memphis, TN 38103, (901) 222-0200. Counter hours are weekdays, eight to half past four. Payments by post go to P.O. Box 2751, Memphis, TN 38101-2751.
  • Board of Equalization: 1075 Mullins Station Road, Suite C-142, Memphis, TN 38134, (901) 222-7300.
  • City of Memphis Treasury: 125 North Main Street, 901-522-1111, for the separate city bill.

Write down each parcel number you own. When a notice goes missing, find the bill on the Trustee's realty tax page using the parcel number.

Housing snapshot

The county counted 910,226 people in July 2025, a 2.1% dip from the 2020 estimates base, living in 409,202 housing units. Owners occupy 54.1% of them. Median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $249,100, and 1,230 building permits were issued in 2025. About 46 percent of homes are rented, which means a landlord selling a rental often has tax and tenant questions an owner-occupant skips. Memphis is the county seat. Bartlett, Germantown, Lakeland, Millington, Arlington and Collierville run their own governments, and some of them send separate tax bills.

How values are set

More than 353,000 real estate parcels are valued by the Assessor, who reappraises every fourth year. 2025 was the most recent round, 2029 is next, and business personal property is revalued annually. Market value is estimated from sales, cost and income data fed into a computer-assisted mass appraisal system.

The state then converts that value into a tax base with a fixed ratio: houses and farms are counted at one quarter of appraised value, and commercial and industrial parcels at 40 percent. The rate is applied to each hundred dollars of that base, and your notice prints the county rate. Within Memphis, the council fixes the city rate and city levies rely on the Assessor's certified values as of each January 1.

Due dates and penalties

This year county bills could be paid starting Monday, October 5, and stay open through February's end. On March 1 the account is delinquent and a charge of 1.5 percent of the base tax lands every month until you pay. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before the last day of February. Installments are fine. Memphis keeps its own calendar: it bills after the City Council sets a rate in mid to late June, and the tax is late once August 31 passes.

Selling a Memphis house means paying off both the county and the city account, so request two payoff figures, one from the Trustee and one from the City Treasury.

How to appeal your assessment

You petition the Shelby County Board of Equalization, the body that reviews the Assessor's values, and there is no fee. Appeals are heard in a window from May 1 to June 30 each year, and the outcome can be a higher value, a lower one, or no change. Miss the window and the disputed value usually stands for the year.

There are three ways to file: the Board's e-file site, a postmarked letter, or a visit to the Board's office on a weekday. The e-file site is live only during appeal season and takes uploaded supporting documents. You will get a hearing notice at least two weeks before the date. Moving a hearing is generally impractical, and every document you rely on must be in hand when you appear. Procedural questions go to (901) 222-7300.

Payment help for fixed-income and delinquent owners

The Trustee's Quarterly Payment Program is meant for retired or unemployed owners aged 65 and over on a fixed income, living in their own Memphis or Shelby County home with no delinquent taxes. Reapply each year, with applications taken July through October. County installments land on October 31, January 31, April 30 and July 31, and Memphis installments on August 31, November 30, February 28 and May 31.

A Written Payment Plan is a different tool for owners who are already delinquent. To qualify, the parcel has to be scheduled for a current tax sale, every delinquent year goes into the plan, the term tops out at 24 months, and each monthly payment is due by the 20th. Call the Tax Sale Department at (901) 222-0200. Older Memphis homeowners can also ask about the city's Tax Relief and Tax Freeze programs. The State of Tennessee resets the income limit annually.

Clearing taxes before closing

Every payoff is checked by the Trustee the day the money comes in, and the lien stays until the balance is fully paid. That is why a closing agent should order a new payoff figure rather than reuse an old one. Interest is totaled through each month's end, but legal fees can be added mid-month, so a closing near the turn of a month deserves care.

State law directs the Trustee to sue for delinquent real estate tax. Memphis turns real estate accounts over to its delinquent attorneys on February 1 once they are a full year behind. If you are behind, call before that date. A quick cash closing can also help, because the lien gets paid from proceeds before more fees pile up.

Seasonal Trustee branches operate in Bartlett, Germantown, Arlington, Collierville, Millington and Raleigh. Year-round payment is at 157 Poplar Avenue, by phone at (901) 222-0200, or by mail.

Pull together the parcel number, your latest notice and proof of any payment plan or exemption before listing. Give copies to the closing agent so the payoff request names the correct county and city accounts.

Frequently asked questions

When is Shelby County property tax due?

You could start paying Monday, October 5, and February's end is the cutoff. March 1 makes it delinquent, and 1.5 percent of the base tax is then added every month.

Does Memphis send a separate property tax bill?

Yes, the city bills separately once the City Council sets its rate, generally in mid to late June, and late status begins after August 31. For the city balance call the City Treasury at 901-522-1111. The Trustee handles the county balance.

When can I appeal my Shelby County property value?

During the May 1 to June 30 window. The Board of Equalization's online filing site works only in that season, so call (901) 222-7300 to confirm the dates for the current year.

How often does Shelby County reappraise?

Real property is reappraised on a four-year cycle, last in 2025 and next in 2029. Business personal property gets a new appraisal each year.

Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Shelby County taxes?

Only if the parcel is scheduled for a current tax sale. The plan has to include every delinquent year, run no longer than 24 months, and have payments in by the 20th monthly. The Tax Sale Department at (901) 222-0200 sets it up.

How do I pay a Rutherford County property tax bill?

You can pay through the Trustee's online portal, by phone, at the counters or by mail. Phone payments go through 1-888-546-4299 and require a seven digit receipt number, padded with leading zeros when it is shorter.

  • In person: both offices take cash, checks, cards, money orders and cashier's checks. Write checks to Rutherford County Trustee.
  • Regular mail: PO Box 1316, Murfreesboro, TN 37133.
  • Overnight delivery: Rutherford County Trustee, Historic Courthouse, Room 102, Murfreesboro, TN 37130.
  • With every payment: add a daytime phone number and your receipt or account number.

Servicers get tax data on request, so if your lender pays from escrow the paper bill is only for your records.

Who is responsible for the tax bill when a house sells?

A new owner should read the closing statement or ask the title company who owes what, because unpaid taxes keep building against the property itself. The yearly bill spans January 1 through December 31.

Business owners follow a similar rule. A business that was operating on January 1 owes personal property tax for the full year, even if it closed before December 31. Call the County Clerk at 615-898-7800 and the Assessor at 615-898-7750 if a business has shut down.

Owners who rent a house by the night face a separate yearly filing with the Assessor, a questionnaire and affidavit due each September for the following tax year. Call the office about the current cycle.

How to contest a Rutherford County assessment

Three steps apply: an Assessor review, the local equalization board, and then the State Board of Equalization. County boards generally open their hearings on June 1.

A state filing must arrive by August 1 or within 45 days after the local board's notice, whichever is later (T.C.A. 67-5-1412(e)). Assessments reflect the situation on January 1. The Assessor's site has a presentation on property values and revaluation, so check it for the current reappraisal cycle.

What the register charges to file your deed

Deeds are billed at $5.00 a page, $10.00 minimum, plus a $2.00 computer fund fee, and the state conveyance tax is $3.70 for each $1,000. A $1.00 fee is collected only when that state tax is paid. The fee list cites T.C.A. 8-21-1001.

Staff at the Register's office do not run title searches and make no promise that a property is free and clear, so leave that step to a title company. The office also offers a MyLandAlert notice service for early warning of land fraud on your parcel.

Relief programs

The Trustee runs two programs, a Senior Tax Freeze and relief for disabled veteran owners and their surviving spouses, and both are limited to a primary residence.

  • Senior Tax Freeze: owners 65 and older lock the tax at the amount for the year they qualify, on up to five acres. The income limit is reset every year and you reapply each time. Remodeling raises the frozen amount, and a sale or lost eligibility puts the house back at current value and rate.
  • Veteran relief: the benefit is figured on only the first $175,000 of market value. Applications are due 35 days after the jurisdiction's delinquency date, and the tax must be paid by then.

A surviving spouse qualifies only if married to the veteran at the time of death and not remarried since.

Settling the bill at a Rutherford County closing

A sale here usually involves one county bill and, for some addresses, a city bill. Work through it in this order.

  1. Ask the Trustee at 615-893-5210 for the balance, and the city office too if the house is in Murfreesboro or La Vergne.
  2. If a lender escrows your tax, confirm with the servicer that the last payment posted.
  3. Give the title company each figure and the closing date, so it can pay from your proceeds.
  4. After closing, keep the settlement statement with your tax records.

A buyer who pays cash and takes the house as-is needs the same payoffs, so having them ready shortens the timeline. If a balance turns out to be larger than you expected, ask the office what it consists of before you agree to a closing date, since interest adds to it each month.

Frequently asked questions

What is Rutherford's 2025 property tax rate?

The county charges $1.8762 on every $100 of assessed value. Smyrna tacks on $0.5257 and Eagleville $0.4051, while Murfreesboro and La Vergne each run their own city collection.

When do Rutherford County property taxes become delinquent?

Once February ends. The bill is payable from the first Monday in October, and each month after the delinquency date adds 1.5 percent interest to what is unpaid.

Does paying early earn a discount in Rutherford County?

No. Paying in October costs the same as paying in February, because the Trustee gives no early payment discount.

Who handles a value dispute in Rutherford County?

Start with the Property Assessor at 615-898-7750. Anything the county board leaves unsettled can go to the State Board of Equalization by the August 1 or 45 day deadline.

Can Rutherford County seniors freeze their tax?

Yes, if you are 65 or older, live in the house and have no more than five acres, and you reapply every year. The Trustee at 615-898-7705 can quote this year's income limit.

Who handles property tax in Blount County

Three bodies share the job: the Property Assessor appraises each parcel, the Board of Commissioners picks the tax rate and the Trustee takes in the money. The Assessor is at 351 Court Street in the Blount County Courthouse, Maryville, TN 37804, phone 865-273-5850. The Trustee is on the third floor at 347 Court Street, phone 865-273-5900. Each office keeps weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The assessor page explains that the office appraises and assesses about 70,000 parcels and audits at least 10 percent of business personal property accounts every year. The assessor does not raise or lower your tax, since what you owe comes from the assessed value times the rate. The Trustee's property tax page makes a similar point: the Trustee collects, and does not set rates or appraisals.

The county includes Maryville, Alcoa, Townsend, Friendsville and Rockford, plus the town of Louisville and part of Vonore. Those figures cover county tax. A city may send its own bill, and its collector might be the city treasurer, the city recorder or the county trustee, so ask the city whether a second bill applies to your address.

Blount County housing snapshot

The county's July 2025 population estimate is 143,820, a 6.3 percent rise since April 2020. Owners live in 77.0 percent of its 64,682 housing units, and the median value for an owner-occupied home is $320,500 (2020 to 2024). Maryville serves as seat and biggest city. Blount County Schools serve everything outside Maryville and Alcoa, which run their own systems, so the school district tied to an address can shape what a house sells for.

How the bill is calculated

Start with the appraised value, apply the assessment percentage for the property type, and multiply the result by the rate per $100 of assessed value. Percentages from the assessor:

  • Residential improvements and residential land: 25 percent of fair market value (land may be assessed on market value or use value)
  • Commercial property: 40 percent of fair market value
  • Commercial business personal property: 30 percent of the appraised value reported on the Tangible Personal Property Schedule

The county rate is $1.29 per $100 for 2026. Earlier rates were $2.47 per $100 from 2015 through 2022 and $1.59 from 2023 through 2025. The commissioners decide the rate.

The Trustee reports how the money is divided: 46.50 percent goes to general county purposes, 42.65 percent to education and 10.85 percent to debt, with over 95 percent of that debt tied to education. Property tax is about 40 percent of what the Trustee collects, and state money, mainly for education, adds another 30 percent.

Due dates, discounts and penalties

How to appeal your assessment

The first stop is the County Board of Equalization, meeting June 1. An assessment that is never taken to the county board usually becomes final. An informal review with the assessor may correct a mistake quickly, but it is not an appeal. Phone 865-273-5850 to ask about one and to be placed on the county board's agenda.

Still unhappy after the county board rules? The State Board of Equalization takes appeals until August 1 of the tax year or for 45 days after the county board's notice was sent, whichever ends later. A late notice means you should confirm your deadline with the State Board at 615-401-7883. An administrative judge hears the matter and has 90 days to rule. The taxpayer has the burden of proof.

Evidence that works:

  • Comparable sales, with adjustments explained for size, age, condition and location
  • An appraisal, which may require the appraiser to testify
  • A stated value of your own, since a bare claim of overvaluation is generally not enough

Before the bill turns delinquent, pay at least the portion you do not dispute, and clear any earlier delinquent years in full. The Comptroller's appeal page shows how to work out the undisputed amount. A higher value after a countywide reappraisal does not by itself prove the assessment is wrong.

Tax relief and freeze programs

Two state programs run through the Trustee's office. Property Tax Relief is a rebate for homeowners 65 or older whose combined income from all sources and all owners, spouse included, is not over $38,470, using 2025 income for tax year 2026. It also reaches totally and permanently disabled taxpayers under the same limit, certain disabled veteran homeowners with service-connected disabilities and the widow of such a veteran.

The Property Tax Freeze lets owners 65 or older by the end of the tax year freeze all or part of their county tax. Applicants must be on the recorded deed, occupy the home as a principal residence and report 2025 combined income of $63,470 or less. Only a limited amount of land qualifies, so a 100-acre farm would freeze only the residence and part of its land. You must apply and be approved every year.

For tax year 2026 the deadline for both programs is April 5, 2027. Call 865-273-5900 to learn which documents to bring.

Selling with taxes owed

Ownership on the tax roll is fixed on January 1, which means the 2026 bill can show the seller's name even if the house closed in the fall. Taxes are normally prorated at closing, and the buyer then carries them. The Trustee tries to mail the notice to the new owner without always knowing who agreed to pay, so a buyer with no notice should call about the parcel.

With back tax outstanding, ask the Trustee for the exact amount soon, since interest of 1.5 percent builds monthly. An unpaid balance, an open appeal or an estate can be sorted out at the closing table, and the title company can walk you through it.

County tax for 2026 is $1.29 per $100 of assessed value, a figure the commissioners set. City tax, where it applies, comes on top.

March 1 is when unpaid tax turns delinquent, following the payment window that closes at the end of February. Interest of 1.5 percent a month then applies. Tax year 2026 relief and freeze applications are due April 5, 2027.

Is there a discount for paying Blount County property tax early?

Yes. Paying by the end of October takes 2 percent off, and paying in November takes 1 percent off. After November no discount applies.

Use the Trustee's office at 347 Court Street in Maryville, the mail, the website, or the phone line at 855-777-3468. Most local banks accept payment until the delinquency date; credit unions cannot. Cards and e-checks cost a convenience fee.

How do I challenge my Blount County property value?

Start with the County Board of Equalization on June 1, then go to the State Board if needed. Come with comparable sales or an appraisal, and keep up payment on the undisputed amount so the account stays current.

Hamilton County at a glance for sellers

Chattanooga, the county seat, anchors Hamilton County and the metro area of southeast Tennessee. Who collects your tax and at what rate depends on which of these your address falls in.

The county had 390,833 people in July 2025, 6.5 percent more than in April 2020. It has 176,983 housing units, and owners occupy 63.9 percent of them. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $312,800 and household income is $76,183. Permits for new building numbered 1,887 in 2025.

Who bills and who collects

One office values, one body sets the rate, and one office collects. The assessor appraises each parcel. The commissioners choose the county rate. The Trustee mails bills and receives payments.

The Trustee sits in Room 210 of the courthouse on Georgia Avenue in Chattanooga and runs a second counter at 6125 Preservation Drive, Suite 101, in the Bonny Oaks Industrial Park. Both open from eight to four on weekdays. Call (423) 209-7270.

The Trustee also bills for Collegedale, East Ridge, Lakesite, Red Bank, Ridgeside, Soddy Daisy and Walden. Chattanooga does its own billing through the City Treasurer at City Hall, 101 E 11th Street, Room 100, at (423) 643-7262 or ptax@chattanooga.gov. A house in Chattanooga therefore gets two separate bills.

The Assessor of Property is at 6135 Heritage Park Drive, (423) 209-7300. The assessor's FAQ points out that the office only sets values. When a bill goes up and the value did not move, the cause is a higher rate.

Property tax rates

After the four-year reappraisal, the county certified a rate of $1.51 per $100 of assessed value, replacing $2.23. The county mayor and the assessor described it as the lowest since 1941. The assessor estimated that roughly two thirds of owners would pay the same or less county tax than they did in 2024. State law forces a lower certified rate after a reappraisal so that rising values do not create a windfall, although local governments may raise it again.

Chattanooga's tax page lists a separate city rate of 1.93 per $100. Houses count at one quarter of appraised value for tax purposes, and commercial buildings at two fifths. For a Chattanooga home, the county bill and the city bill each come from assessed value over 100 times that body's rate. Phone the Trustee to learn the rate printed on this year's notice.

If your home is in Chattanooga, budget for both bills when you compare listings or estimate a buyer's monthly cost. A home in one of the other cities served by the Trustee carries the county bill plus whatever that city adds.

Due dates and late penalties

Bills are mailed in late September. You can pay starting October 1, and the window runs to the end of February. From March 1 the county adds 1.5 percent per month, or 18 percent a year in its own description.

No state rule makes the county mail a notice, and a missing one does not erase interest. How to challenge your value

Still unhappy? The assessor's office can give you the form to go before the county Board of Equalization. That board meets during June and takes filings into the first week of the month, so confirm the closing date by phone. A later stage is the State Board of Equalization, where an administrative judge hears the case. The owner has to prove the number, and matched sales of similar homes make the strongest evidence.

Tennessee refunds a slice of the tax to low-income seniors, disabled homeowners and disabled military service members. The county's FAQ quotes a $37,530 income ceiling for 2025. Hamilton County says it matches what the state pays. To book a time, call the Bonny Oaks office at (423) 209-7799.

The freeze for owners 65 and older follows different lines. The county government is missing from the state's list of 28 freeze counties, yet Chattanooga adopted one in 2017 and uses a 2026 income limit of $63,470. It reduces only the city bill. As a seller, request the balance for every tax year from the Trustee's office before you list, and the city balance too if you are in Chattanooga.

Inherited the home, or behind on the bill? The title company can settle the debt from your proceeds at closing. The Register of Deeds, reachable at (423) 209-6560, records the deed and collects the state transfer tax.

Every four years. The most recent was in 2025 and the next is 2029. Between reappraisals, a record error can still be corrected on request.

Do I pay both Chattanooga and Hamilton County property tax?

Yes, a Chattanooga owner gets a county bill from the Trustee and a separate city bill from the City Treasurer. The Trustee also collects for seven other cities, among them East Ridge and Soddy Daisy.

Houses within Bristol, Kingsport or Bluff City can carry a second, city bill. The Trustee's FAQ covers this. The city sets its own rate and due date, so ask city hall.

Housing in Sullivan County

Up in Tennessee's northeast corner on the Virginia line, Sullivan County is home to Kingsport, its largest city, plus Bristol, Bluff City and part of Johnson City. Blountville serves as county seat. Because three school systems operate here (Bristol Tennessee City Schools, Kingsport City School District and Sullivan County Schools), the zone a buyer gets depends on the address.

How the tax bill is figured

The Trustee's FAQ gives the formula: assessed value is 25 percent of the property's value, and the county rate is applied to that figure. For 2025 the posted county rate is $1.6129 per $100 of assessed value, and a city can add its own levy.

A bill covers a single calendar year. Business furniture and equipment are taxable as well, and business owners file a personal property schedule annually. Property values will be reset in the next county-wide reappraisal, scheduled for 2027.

State guidance favors sales of comparable homes, with the gaps in size, age, condition and location accounted for. You can add an appraisal. Go to the Trustee in Blountville, or use the Bristol and Kingsport counters during their October 1 to March 15 season. Bank of Tennessee branches accept cash or checks if you bring the notice.

Leniency is not on offer here. T.C.A. 67-5-2803 strips the Trustee of any power to waive, prorate or release tax or interest, so a late bill simply stays late.

Market context for sellers

This is a high-value Middle Tennessee market. The population reached 272,061 in July 2025, a 9.8% rise over the April 2020 base. There are 103,674 housing units, and owners live in 78.8% of the occupied ones. A typical owned home is valued at $751,900, and builders pulled 1,621 permits in 2025. Brentwood and Franklin anchor the north end, while the south keeps more of its farm feel. Williamson County Schools serves most of the county, and part of Franklin sends kindergarten through eighth graders to the Franklin Special School District.

How the tax is figured

Tennessee fixes the share of appraised value that gets taxed: 25 percent on a house, 40 percent on commercial and industrial buildings, 30 percent on business personal property. Your rate multiplies each $100 of that taxed share, so a bigger appraisal means a bigger bill. Your appraisal is the number worth checking, because everything else follows from it.

The 2026 rates appear as a chart on the county's Property Tax Rates page. Add the county rate to whichever city or school district covers your address to see the full picture. New construction is valued through September 1, and then the rolls move to the Trustee.

The roll goes public in May. If your value changed, a notice arrives by mail. Reading it right away leaves time to act before hearings begin in June.

Escrow customers still get a statement, which the Trustee calls a copy for your records. Phone ahead to learn which payment methods the 2026 bill accepts, and take the bill or your parcel details if you pay in person.

Two rules matter once you plan to sell. The mailing follows whoever owned the parcel on January 1, so a seller who has already sold should give the bill to the buyer. And the counter staff cannot wipe out interest.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin with a call to the Assessor at 615-790-5708 and ask how your figure was built. Plenty of disagreements end in that conversation. Even so, you must reserve a hearing time with the county equalization board to protect your appeal rights. The board has five residents, each appointed by the County Commission for two years. It meets in June, and the Assessor's staff want calls during the first week of June. Filing is limited to the person on the roll, an authorized agent or the owner.

After the county hearing, the State Board of Equalization is the next step. Filings are accepted until August 1 of the tax year, or 45 days after the county notice if that is later. Selling with taxes owed

Whoever holds title on January 1 is the name on the statement. An autumn closing therefore leaves the 2026 mailing in your mailbox, and you owe the buyer that paper. Look at the closing statement to see how the title company divides the year. Ask for that breakdown early, since the split depends on the contract terms and the day you close.

Try this order. Ring the Trustee before a contract is signed and get the amount currently due on the parcel. Pass it to whoever runs your closing, whether that is a title company or an attorney, so the county is paid out of the sale money in one move. File the receipt with your sale papers. Freeze participants should talk to the Trustee before listing, because a sale followed by a purchase resets the base amount.

Late tax keeps growing each month after March 1, and the Trustee cannot trim it. Buyers who finance will have lenders asking for a current account, so pay off any balance ahead of closing. A cash purchase avoids that lender check and the underwriting wait, though the county balance still gets paid at the table.

Suite 203 of the building at 1320 West Main Street in Franklin. Hours are 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays, and the phone is 615-790-5709.

No. The Trustee has no legal power to excuse, split or cancel tax or interest.

How much income can I have for the freeze?

The 2026 ceiling is $69,150, counting everyone's 2025 income on the application. Applicants need to be 65 by the last day of 2026.

The Assessor answers at 615-790-5708. Reaching the county equalization board means calling in the first week of June.

  • Trustee: One Public Square, Columbia, TN 38401, 931-375-2201. Make checks out to Maury County Trustee and mail them to that address.
  • Assessor of Property: 6 Public Square, Columbia, TN 38401, 931-375-4001.

The person who held title on New Year's Day gets the bill, and new mailing addresses go to the Assessor, as the Trustee's page explains. Living in Columbia, Spring Hill or Mount Pleasant? Check with that city's hall for a separate city bill.

Maury County market snapshot

Maury County lies south of Nashville and has grown fast. Columbia holds the courthouse, and Spring Hill, which straddles the Williamson County line, is the largest city. The county counted 118,131 people on July 1, 2025, up 17.0% from April 2020, and has 49,725 housing units, 70.9% of them owner-occupied. A typical owner-occupied house is valued at $355,700, typical rent is $1,300, and the median household earns $76,130. Builders pulled 1,408 permits in 2025.

Interstate 65, State Route 396 and US 31 tie the county to Nashville, which explains much of the demand. Maury County Public Schools runs the public schools countywide. For a seller, fast growth means buyers are comparing many new listings, so a clean tax record and an accurate assessment help your house hold its own.

The 2026 reappraisal

Maury County values every property afresh on a four-year rhythm, and this is one of those years. The figure on file reflects what the market was paying on January 1, 2026, with later improvements layered on at equalized value. Because prices have risen a lot, anyone whose house was last valued before that run-up should study the new notice.

The arithmetic is brief: appraised value times the ratio for the property class, then the rate applied to every $100 of that. Houses are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value statewide.

The county's 2025 to 2026 budget letter to the state Comptroller shows a rate of $1.91 for each $100 of assessment, with no increase for residents. A reappraisal year can bring a different rate, so ask the Trustee which one is on your current bill. The Assessor's page explains the calculation and links to reappraisal guides.

Payment window and late charges

You can start paying in early October and have until the end of February, and bills are due as soon as you receive them. Starting March 1, penalty and interest of 1.5 percent accrue and keep growing monthly. On April 1, any account still open is sent to Chancery Court.

Part payments are fine with the Trustee, but whatever is unpaid on March 1 starts earning interest. The postmark date counts as your payment date, apart from accounts already moved to Chancery Court. A county is not required to mail notices under Tennessee law, so you cannot dodge the charges by pointing to a bill that never came.

  • By mail to Maury County Trustee, One Public Square, Columbia, TN 38401

How to contest a new value

Climb three steps in order: the Assessor, the county equalization board, then the state board. For this year's county board process, call 931-375-4001.

The later steps are laid out in the state's appeals guide. Skip the county board and the value usually becomes final. Your state deadline is August 1 or the 45th day after the county board mailed notice, whichever comes later, so count from the mailing date if your county notice was late. After the hearing an administrative judge has 90 days to rule, and a court petition must be filed within 60 days of the state order becoming final.

An informal review, where an assessor offers one, can speed up a fix, yet it is not an appeal and preserves no rights. Ask whether Maury's office does one, and file with the county board regardless.

Before you call the Assessor, write down your parcel number, the value on the notice, and why you think it is off. Pull sales of similar houses nearby, note any differences in size, age and condition, and keep photos of problems such as a worn roof or foundation cracks. Specific evidence makes the conversation shorter and gives the county board something concrete to weigh.

Tax relief and monthly payments

The Trustee's office helps elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled-veteran owners and the widows or widowers of a disabled veteran apply for the Tennessee Tax Relief Program under state guidelines. Call 931-375-2201 for the forms and the current income limits.

Through the ACH program, the bill can be split into equal monthly bank debits; call that number to enroll. Splitting it avoids one large payment in February, though every debit has to clear before March 1 charges begin.

What a sale changes

Tax years match calendar years, and the January 1 owner receives the notice. After a fall sale the seller's name stays on the bill, although the buyer takes the house into the next year. Ask the Trustee for the exact balance and have the title agent divide it at closing.

A seller who lists late has little time, since charges begin in March and Chancery Court follows in April. Whatever is open at closing is deducted from your net proceeds. Confirm the figure with the Trustee about a week before.

Gather four things before you list: the latest bill, proof of any monthly debits, relief paperwork, and the Assessor's value notice. A house held by a family for years deserves a look at older years too, since a balance may be hiding there. Cash buyers can close quickly, and the Trustee's payoff is still paid at the table. Keep copies of every receipt, because the title agent may ask for proof that a payment cleared. If a bill is already late, call the Trustee at 931-375-2201 for a current figure rather than relying on an old statement, since interest grows every month.

Frequently asked questions

Is 2026 a reappraisal year in Maury County?

Yes. A new appraisal comes every four years, and the current one is 2026, based on market prices as of January 1.

What rate does Maury County use?

The 2025 to 2026 budget letter lists $1.91 per $100 of assessed value. Since the Commission sets it, confirm the figure on your bill or with the Trustee.

When do Maury County taxes become late?

March 1 is when charges of 1.5 percent a month begin, and April 1 is when delinquent accounts go to Chancery Court. You can pay from the first Monday in October through February.

Does Maury County accept partial payments?

Yes. Any balance left on March 1 still accrues interest, so a part payment shrinks the amount earning interest without stopping it.

Where do I send a new mailing address?

Tell the Assessor, at 931-375-4001. The Trustee sends address changes there, and a missing bill does not cancel penalty or interest.

Which office does what

Property tax here runs through three desks at the Sevier County Courthouse, 125 Court Avenue, Sevierville. The Assessor decides what your property is worth, the County Commission picks the rate, and the Trustee sends the bill and takes payment. Match your question to the right desk and you skip a lot of stair climbing.

Sevierville, Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg lie within the county lines. Check with the city hall for your address to learn whether you also get a city bill.

Market context for sellers

Population stands at 101,342 as of July 2025, spread across 62,724 housing units. About 70.7% of households own their home, and owner-occupied homes carry a typical value of $299,000. Builders pulled 1,139 permits in 2025. Cabin rentals have multiplied around Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge, so plenty of sellers own a nightly rental instead of a primary residence. The Assessor offers an online filing for nightly rentals, and the county website has a short-term rental tax estimator next to the primary home and vacant land estimators.

What goes into the bill

The formula has three steps: appraised value, times a state-mandated assessment ratio, times the local rate. Houses and farmland are assessed at one quarter of appraisal, while commercial and industrial land is assessed at 40 percent. Rates are quoted for each hundred dollars of assessed value, and the Trustee's FAQ showed $1.48 for 2024.

Values are reset every five years, and 2026 is a reappraisal year. The Assessor reviews roughly 90,000 parcels. A certified rate is then worked out under state law so that total collections hold steady, and the Board of Commissioners adopts the final figure. Some owners will pay more and some less, so read your own 2026 bill.

Between cycles your value stays fixed unless the building or land physically changes. Changing hands does not reset it.

Bills for 2026 went out in early October. You may pay any time from October 1 and owe no penalty until the end of February 2027. A mailed check must carry a postmark on or before the last day, and the Trustee will not accept an office meter date. Card and e-check payments count on the day you make them. You can pay in installments, and interest applies only to what is left.

Build your file first. Useful items are recent sales of comparable houses, contractor estimates for defects the appraisal overlooked, and corrections to square footage or condition. Relief applies to city taxes as well. Greenbelt is a separate break for parcels of 15 acres or more in farm or forestry use, requested by March 1, and land that leaves the program owes a rollback of three years of savings. Selling with taxes owed

A tax lien stays with the parcel, so whatever is owed must be paid at or before closing. The Trustee bills whoever is listed as owner, and buyers are pointed to the closing statement to see who covers that year's tax. The title company normally pays an open balance at the table from your proceeds.

Once the deadline passes, the account is delinquent and goes to Chancery Court, where costs get added and the parcel may be advertised for the annual auction. The Clerk and Master posts the list 20 to 30 days before the sale. Bidders sign in at the courthouse 30 minutes before it begins and pay with cash, money order or check. The former owner can still redeem for a year, and the winning bidder earns 1 percent a month while waiting.

Owe back taxes? Phone the Trustee at (865) 453-2767 before your name reaches the list. A cash sale skips listing prep, showings and lender delays, so it can close fast enough to clear the balance ahead of the auction. Who mails the property tax bill in Sevier County?

Bills come from the Trustee, usually in the first week of October. Valuing is the Assessor's job and rate-setting belongs to the County Commission, but payment goes to the Trustee at 125 Court Avenue, Room 212W. If nothing arrives, call (865) 453-2767.

What is the deadline for paying Sevier County property tax without interest?

February's last day, which means February 2027 for the 2026 bill. From March 1, interest runs at 1.5 percent a month (18 percent a year), and a postmark after the deadline is treated as late.

Can I pay Sevier County property tax in pieces?

Yes. Partial payments are welcome, and once an account is delinquent, interest accrues only on the remaining balance. Owners 65 or older may also qualify for Tax Relief or Tax Freeze, both applied for in person at the Trustee's office.

How often does Sevier County reappraise?

On a five-year cycle, and this is the year for it. Between cycles a value holds unless the property physically changes. When the new values are set, a certified rate keeps overall collections steady.

Will an unpaid Sevier County tax bill stop a sale?

No, but the balance gets paid out of your sale money because the lien rides with the parcel. Ask the Trustee for the exact payoff on closing day. Once an account reaches Chancery Court it collects costs and can end in a tax sale.

Hamblen County housing snapshot

Hamblen County is small, at 176 square miles, and daily life centers on Morristown, the seat and largest city. Other named places include White Pine, Russellville, Whitesburg, Talbott, Lowland and Witt. Interstate 81, US 11E and US 25E cross the county.

The assessor appraises, state law applies a ratio, and the rate does the rest. Assessed value is 25 percent of appraised value for houses and farms, 40 percent for commercial and industrial property.

Check the notice you receive each year for the appraised value, and compare it with what similar houses nearby have sold for. If your number looks high, that comparison is the start of an appeal. Ask the trustee whether the city sends a separate bill for your address.

How to contest your value

Tax freeze and state relief

Hamblen has both. Under the state relief program, low-income seniors, disabled owners and some disabled military service members get part of the tax refunded. The 2026 ceiling is $38,470 of 2025 income. Refunds for seniors and disabled owners cover up to $33,600 of value, and the figure for disabled military service members is $175,000. Applications go to the trustee, who must receive them within 35 days of the delinquency date.

Hamblen is also on the state's list of 28 counties with a freeze. It joined in 2007, and the 2026 income limit is $39,260. A homeowner who reaches 65 by year end and passes the income test can lock the tax on a main residence at the first qualifying year's amount. Each year requires a new application, and the fixed amount grows if the owner improves the property or moves to a different house.

Before you sell

Ownership is measured on January 1, yet the title company divides the year's bill between buyer and seller at closing. Ask the trustee for your balance before you list. That matters most for an inherited house or one with several unpaid years, since interest starts once March 1 goes by.

The Clerk and Master, at 423-586-9112, keeps a delinquent tax section on its website, along with a tax search and payment tool. After closing, take the deed to the Register of Deeds, also in the courthouse, where the state recording taxes are paid.

A short plan helps. Call the trustee at 423-586-6290 and ask for the balance on every year, not just the current one. Call the assessor at 423-586-1852 and confirm the name and parcel details on your record. If you plan to dispute the value, remember that the local board opens June 1 and that you still owe the undisputed part of the bill. If the house is vacant or inherited, note that the delinquency clock runs from March 1 whether or not anyone lives there. A cash buyer can often close quickly enough to pay arrears from proceeds before the bill grows.

For a lender-financed buyer, the title company will want a clear balance. For a cash sale, the same balance still gets cleared from your proceeds at closing. Either way, keep your last bill and your deed handy when you call, since staff may ask for the parcel or owner name.

When are Hamblen County property taxes due?

The county's tax page gives October 1. Bills turn delinquent the following March 1. Payment is taken at the courthouse counter, at the Davy Crockett Parkway satellite office, or through TNPayments.com/Hamblen.

Who do I call about my Hamblen County property assessment?

The assessor's office, 511 West Second North Street, Morristown. The number is 423-586-1852. The office values roughly 32,000 parcels.

Does Hamblen County have a property tax freeze?

Yes, adopted in 2007, with a 2026 income limit of $39,260. Applicants must be 65 by the end of the year, own and live in the home, and reapply with the trustee each year.

How do I dispute my Hamblen County property value?

Call the assessor, then go before the local equalization board, which opens June 1. After that, the state board takes an appeal filed by August 1 or within forty-five days of the local notice, whichever comes later.

Where can I pay Hamblen County property tax online?

Use TNPayments.com/Hamblen, the link on the county's tax page. For balance questions, call the trustee at 423-586-6290.

Who bills and collects property tax

Two offices in the Rogersville courthouse annex split the work. The Property Assessor decides the value. The Trustee takes that value and the commission's rate, makes the bill and collects it. Tax bills usually go out after the County Commission sets the rate and passes the budget, normally no later than October 15.

The Trustee's office is at 110 East Main Street, Room 203, Rogersville, TN 37857, phone (423) 272-7022. The Assessor is at 110 East Main Street, Room 201, phone (423) 272-8505. Weekday hours for both are eight to four, though the Trustee closes for lunch between noon and one.

Due dates, late interest and payment options

No interest is charged on payments made October 1 through the end of February. From March 1, any open balance picks up 1.5% a month.

The Trustee accepts partial payments, but the owner must sign a form each tax year before the first partial payment is taken. Cash, check, money order and debit or credit cards (Mastercard or Visa) are accepted. A card payment carries a 2.65% processing fee plus a $1.00 convenience fee. A satellite office at 150 South Central in Church Hill, phone (423) 357-4350, opens for the season from mid-October to mid-March. How a Hawkins County tax bill is figured

Three steps make a bill: the assessor provides the assessed value, the commission sets the rate, and the Trustee multiplies them. The Trustee's page includes a tax calculator if you want to test a figure before the bills arrive.

The commission has 14 members, two from each of seven civil districts, and it adopts the rate along with the annual budget for the general, school and highway funds. A higher rate is a public decision with notices and hearings, so the commission's budget meetings before bills go out are the time to speak.

Appealing your assessment

Start with the Assessor's office at (423) 272-8505 and ask for an informal review. Show why the value is too high, with sales of comparable homes or an appraisal. When the review fails, the next stops are the county Board of Equalization and then the State Board of Equalization. The assessor's page warns that deadlines are strictly enforced.

The county board hears cases in June each year. Assessment change notices go out in May, so watch your mail in spring, since a notice is sent only when a value changed.

  • A reappraisal updates values to current sales, and Tennessee Code 67-5-1601 requires the cycle.
  • After a reappraisal, the State Board of Equalization certifies a tax rate meant to bring in the same revenue as the year before, apart from new construction.
  • If the County Commission adopts a higher rate than the certified one, that counts as a tax increase and needs public notice and hearings.

Gather your evidence before you call: recent sale prices of similar homes nearby, photos of defects, and any appraisal you already have. The more specific the dollar figure you propose, the easier it is for the assessor or the board to act on it.

Tax relief for homeowners

Tennessee offers relief to elderly and disabled homeowners and disabled military service members. Applications go to the Hawkins County Trustee. Income counts, and proof of income is required. The application must be completed no later than April 4 after the February 28 payment deadline.

Relief is a reimbursement from the state toward taxes already owed, not an exemption. You still receive a bill and must pay it. Relief covers only your primary residence, and the amount changes with your assessment and tax rate. The statutes are Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-701 through 67-5-704.

Farm and forest owners can ask about greenbelt. Apply by March 15. If land later stops qualifying, a roll-back tax equal to three years of savings comes due.

Because the program pays you back after the bill is settled, do not skip or delay your payment while you wait for approval. Keep your receipt, since it supports the application.

Selling with unpaid taxes

A tax debt follows the parcel, which means the title company must get a payoff from the Trustee ahead of closing. Request a figure good through the expected closing date, with interest after March 1 included.

Taxes that stay unpaid are collected through the Hawkins County Chancery Court. The Clerk and Master, at 100 E. Main Street, Suite 316, Rogersville, collects delinquent property tax for the county and the towns. The number for delinquent tax questions is (423) 272-8150. The office keeps a delinquent tax sale list and offers online delinquent tax payments, searchable by parcel number.

Behind on taxes? Phone the Clerk and Master to learn whether your parcel is on the list.

A short routine keeps a Hawkins County sale on track. Call the Trustee at (423) 272-7022 for a payoff through your expected closing date. Call the Assessor at (423) 272-8505 to confirm the owner name and parcel details. If a past-due balance exists, ask the Clerk and Master whether the parcel has reached the delinquent list. Give the title company the payoff figure so it can pay the Trustee out of your proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can often close quickly enough to clear the balance before more interest builds.

Hawkins County for homeowners and sellers

Hawkins County covers about 500 square miles in the northeast corner of Tennessee, with Rogersville as the county seat. Church Hill is the largest city. Bulls Gap, Mount Carmel and Surgoinsville are towns, and Bean Station and Kingsport reach into the county.

There are 59,559 residents and about 28,006 housing units. Roughly 80.1% of homes are owner-occupied, valued at a median $176,300. Gross rent has a median of $785, household income $56,936, and monthly owner costs with a mortgage $1,136.

  • The county government does not issue building permits and has no zoning restrictions or code enforcement. Permits come through the State of Tennessee.
  • Septic records, if you need them for a sale, come from the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation. You may need the name of the original owner.
  • New 911 address questions go to (423) 272-7532.
  • School districts serving the county are Hawkins County, Kingsport City and Rogersville City, which covers elementary grades only.

Where do I pay Hawkins County property taxes?

Pay the Hawkins County Trustee at 110 East Main Street, Room 203, Rogersville, or at the Church Hill office from mid-October to mid-March. Online payment is linked from the county home page. Card payments add a 2.65% fee plus $1.00.

When do Hawkins County property taxes become delinquent?

Delinquency begins once February ends. Interest of 1.5% per month is added from March 1. The Trustee accepts partial payments if the owner signs the required form for that tax year.

How do I reach the Hawkins County Property Assessor?

The office is at 110 East Main Street, Room 201, Rogersville, and the phone number is (423) 272-8505. It opens at eight and closes at four on weekdays.

When can I appeal a Hawkins County assessment?

The county Board of Equalization meets each June, after change notices go out in May. The assessor's office handles informal reviews first.

Who handles delinquent tax sales in Hawkins County?

The Chancery Court Clerk and Master handles them. Call (423) 272-8150 for delinquent tax questions. The office keeps a delinquent tax sale list.

Who sends and who sets the bill

Three roles split the work: the Assessor of Property appraises land and buildings, the County Commission chooses the rate, and the Trustee takes in the money. Appraisals and rate-setting are outside the Trustee's job. Value questions go to the Assessor at 423-753-1671. If you think your house is worth less than the roll says, that is the first call to make, well before the bill arrives.

The Trustee runs two counters. The Jonesborough office is in the Historic Courthouse downtown, phone 423-753-1602, open weekdays 8 to 4:30, with a drop box at the corner of the courthouse. The Johnson City office is at 378 Marketplace Boulevard, phone 423-610-7211, open 8:30 to 4:30. Mail goes to PO Box 215, Jonesborough, TN 37659.

County tax is only part of the picture. A house in Johnson City or the Town of Jonesborough also owes city property tax, which means two bills.

What buyers pay for here

Jonesborough is the seat of government and Johnson City is the largest city, with East Tennessee State University and a regional medical center. Buyers choose between Washington County Schools and Johnson City Schools, which serves most of that city, so the address decides the district.

The county counted 141,199 people in July 2025, a 6.2% gain over April 2020, and has 64,564 housing units, with owners in 64.5% of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $249,000 for 2020 to 2024, and 697 building permits were issued in 2025. After the Hurricane Helene flooding of 2024, the Assessor's office asked affected owners to return a reassessment form so values could be adjusted.

How the tax on a house is calculated

The calculation has three steps. Start with the appraised value, take 25 percent of it for residential property (40 percent for commercial), and apply the rate to each $100 of the result. The County Commission has rounded bills to the nearest dollar since tax year 2020.

The Trustee's page shows $2.15 for each $100, labeled as the 2023 county rate. Ask the Trustee for the current figure before you rely on it, since the rate can change from one year to the next. The rate splits among these funds:

Due dates and how to pay

Bills are typically mailed in October, and payment is open until the end of February. Many owners pay in the fall so the receipt is on file before a spring listing. Keep the receipt and the bill number, because a buyer's agent or title company may ask to see them. A balance still open on March 1 gets 1.5 percent interest, added each month. The Trustee wants taxes paid on time whether or not a notice shows up, and asks anyone who has not received one by November 15 to call 423-753-1602. The exception is a mortgage escrow customer, whose lender pays.

  • Online at washington.paytntaxes.com, entering the tax year and bill number

The Trustee also allows partial and prepaid payments, handled at the two offices. Unpaid balances after the delinquency period move to the Clerk and Master for collection, so ask the Trustee how that date works for the current year before letting a bill slide.

Appealing a value that looks too high

The assessment roll goes on public view each May, and owners whose values changed get a mailed notice. If the figure looks higher than what your house would sell for, bring it to the county's Board of Equalization, which hears the case and finalizes the roll. Call 423-753-1671 to ask about the board's schedule and to request an informal look at the value.

If the county board rules against you, the state is the next stop. That filing window closes August 1 or 45 days after the county mailed its notice, whichever is later. Keep paying the part of the bill you do not dispute. Evidence that works includes sales of similar homes, a professional appraisal and a clearly stated value, and you must make the case before an administrative judge.

Tax relief programs

Tax Relief, a state program dating to 1973, pays back part of the tax for qualified elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled former service members and their surviving spouses. The county matches the state amount, up to what was billed. A person rated 100 percent disabled qualifies, and the benefit passes to a surviving spouse. It works as a reimbursement, not an exemption, which means you pay the bill first.

Take a driver's license, Medicare card, Social Security card and last year's income proof when you apply. Selling and the tax bill

Under state law the roll is fixed on January 1, which makes the person listed that day the owner of record for the year. Once a house sells, the Trustee tries to send the buyer a notice, because the office has no way of knowing who agreed to pay what. The usual practice is to prorate at closing and make the buyer responsible afterward. Buyers without a notice should call and check the parcel.

If you still owe tax, the Trustee can give you the exact payoff with interest, and the title company then puts that figure on the settlement statement. Request it close to the closing date, because interest is added monthly after February. Line up these items before you sell:

  • The tax year and bill number for each parcel, which are needed to pay online
  • Any relief voucher that has not yet been returned for the year
  • Whether a Johnson City or Jonesborough city bill is also open

If you are selling a house that flooded in 2024, ask the Assessor whether the reassessment was completed, since a lower value changes what the buyer will owe next year. A cash sale can close before March 1 interest begins to build, which is worth considering if you are behind. Whatever the buyer's financing, clear the balance with the Trustee before the closing date so nothing is left on the parcel.

Pay at the Jonesborough office in the Historic Courthouse or the Johnson City office at 378 Marketplace Boulevard. Online and phone payment also work.

Call the Trustee at 423-753-1602. The office asks owners to call if no notice has arrived by November 15, and owners are expected to pay on time either way.

How is Washington County property tax calculated?

Multiply the appraised value by 25 percent for a home, then multiply by $2.15 per $100. Bills are rounded to the nearest dollar.

Who sets my home's value in Washington County?

The Assessor of Property does, at 423-753-1671. The Trustee only collects the tax.

Offices that value and bill Montgomery County property

Both offices operate from one address, 350 Pageant Lane in Clarksville. The Assessor of Property works from Suite 101-C and puts a value on every parcel. The County Trustee sits in Suite 101-B and sends the bills.

  • Assessor of Property: 931-648-5709, counter open 8 to 4:30 on weekdays.
  • County Trustee: 931-648-5717, open weekdays from half past seven until 4:30.
  • Delinquent tax suits: the Clerk and Master of the Montgomery Chancery Court, 2 Millennium Plaza, Suite 101, 931-648-5703.

Commissioners adopt the rate each year, and the Trustee applies it to every $100 of assessed value. A house inside Clarksville limits also receives a bill from the City of Clarksville, so a seller there has two balances to clear.

Montgomery County housing in brief

Clarksville is the county seat and the only incorporated municipality in Montgomery County, which belongs to the Clarksville, TN-KY metro area. The Census estimate for July 2025 is 249,935 residents, up 13.6% from 220,012 at the 2020 base. The county has 102,547 housing units, and owners live in 61.9% of homes. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $280,200, median household income is $75,613 and median gross rent is $1,308.

Because most homes here are owned rather than rented, a seller is usually dealing with a single owner-occupied bill, plus a city bill if the house is inside Clarksville. Before you pick a list price, learn which of those two bills applies to your address and whether either one has money still owed on it. A quick call to the Trustee at 931-648-5717 answers the county half, and the city Finance and Revenue Department answers the rest.

2026 tax rates and how a bill is figured

The county rate for 2026 is $2.10 per $100 of assessed value, and Clarksville's rate is $1.01. A property inside the city therefore carries a combined $3.11 per $100, while a house outside the city pays the county rate alone.

How a parcel is used decides what share of its appraisal gets taxed. The Trustee's method is to multiply the appraisal by the class percentage, divide by 100, then multiply by the rate.

The sums come out differently for every parcel, so check this arithmetic against the notice mailed to you. Anything that changes the class of your land, such as farm use, or an approved relief program, moves the final figure.

When is the bill due, and what does paying late cost?

Bills go out by mail in the last week of October. Payment opens the first Monday in October and closes on the last day of February with no interest. From March 1, each month adds 1.5 percent to the base tax, which works out to 18 percent a year.

State law does not oblige the Trustee to mail notices, and the county will not excuse lateness because a bill went missing. If you have not received one by early November, call and ask. Partial payments toward the current year can start July 10, provided the balance is cleared by the February cutoff. A payment sent through the Postal Service counts on its postmark date, but an office meter stamp does not.

Online e-checks carry a 1.75 percent plus $1 charge, and Visa or MasterCard payments carry 2.65 percent plus $1. Only the counter takes cash. A handful of neighborhood banks take current-year payments until February 28, as long as you carry the original bill or a printout from the Trustee's website.

City tax has its own ladder. Once an account is twelve months behind, Clarksville refers it to a delinquent tax attorney, and any later payment is made to the Clerk and Master at the chancery court.

How to contest a Montgomery County valuation

Begin by calling the Assessor, 931-648-5709. A miscounted room or wrong land class is frequently fixed on that one call. Disputes that survive go to the county equalization board, which starts its session on the first business day of June and keeps meeting until its docket is done.

Hearing slots are booked through the Assessor, and the phone window runs from May 15 to May 31. The board has five property owners from around the county, and state law reserves two seats for Clarksville residents. You can appear yourself or send a relative, lawyer or authorized agent. Bring appraisals, repair bills and comparable assessments, and skip arguments about what you can afford, since the board weighs value only.

You should get the board's decision letter ahead of July. If you still disagree, the State Board of Equalization takes the next appeal, which must reach it by August 1 or 45 days after the county mailing, whichever falls later. The countywide reappraisal is next due in 2029.

Tax relief and special bills that affect a sale

Tennessee's relief program refunds part of the tax for low-income elderly owners, disabled owners, and disabled veteran owners with their surviving spouses. It works as a reimbursement, so you still receive the bill and pay it. Only the home you live in qualifies, and a house held in an irrevocable trust is left out.

In Clarksville, the Trustee's office is where you sign up for the Tax Freeze program. Relief applications are available at both the county Trustee and the city Finance and Revenue Department. Approved owners get a voucher with each bill and must send it in every year to both offices.

Greenbelt land brings another charge. If a sale ends the farm, forest or open-space classification, rollback taxes for the previous three years (five for open space) come due, and unless the contract says otherwise the seller owes them. A buyer who promises to keep the classification has 90 days after the sale to file the form with the Assessor, or the rollback becomes the buyer's problem. Whichever side owes it, an unpaid rollback attaches to the land as a first lien.
