How does the tax get settled at closing?

New owners are told to check the closing statement or ask the title company about the year's tax. Whatever the purchase contract says, unpaid tax keeps building on the house itself, and a delinquent Clarksville property can still be sent to a tax auction.

  1. Request a balance from the Trustee for county tax and from city Finance and Revenue for city tax.
  2. Find out whether your lender already paid from escrow, because the city refunds a double payment to whoever paid last.
  3. Give the title company both figures so it can pay any remaining balance out of your proceeds.
  4. Check that the closing statement shows the county and city lines separately for a Clarksville address.

If a payoff looks larger than expected, ask the office for a year-by-year breakdown ahead of closing day instead of at the table. Buyers who pay cash and take the house as-is still want those same payoffs, and having them in hand early lets the closing date stay put.

Frequently asked questions

What are the 2026 property tax rates in Montgomery County?

Countywide the levy is $2.10 on each $100 of assessed value, and homes inside Clarksville add the city's $1.01. Houses are assessed at a quarter of appraised value.

What is the deadline to pay Montgomery County tax without interest?

February's final day. Payments open the first Monday of October, and every month beginning March 1 adds 1.5 percent to the base tax.

Where do I start if my Montgomery County valuation looks too high?

Ring the Assessor at 931-648-5709 first. Failing that, request a June hearing before the county equalization board during the May 15 to May 31 call window, then move up to the State Board of Equalization if needed.

Does a Clarksville house owe both city and county tax?

Yes, through two separate bills. The Trustee collects the county share and the city sends its own, while homes outside city limits owe only the county portion.

Who owes the tax when a Montgomery County house sells?

Buyer and seller divide it under the sale contract and closing statement. Because the tax follows the calendar year and the property, ask the title company to confirm the split and clear any balance on closing day.

Offices that handle Roane County property tax

A Roane County tax bill passes through three offices, and every one is in the courthouse at 200 E. Race Street, Kingston. Land values come from the Assessor of Property, payments go to the Trustee, and a bill left unpaid long enough lands with the Clerk and Master.

  • Assessor of Property, Suite 5, 865-376-4362: values, ownership updates, greenbelt and tax freeze paperwork
  • Trustee, Suite 4, 865-376-4938 (mail to P.O. Box 296, Kingston, TN 37763): bills, payments, tax relief applications
  • Clerk and Master, Suite 12, 865-376-2487: delinquent taxes after a lawsuit is filed

Owners often assume the Trustee sets the rate or the appraisal, but it does neither. Take a value dispute to the Assessor and the county Board of Equalization, and a rate complaint to the County Commission.

2026 property tax rates in Roane County

A house inside a city pays the county rate of $1.4523 plus that city's rate, per $100 of assessed value. A house outside every city pays the rural county rate of $1.4987. Tennessee assesses residential property at 25 percent of appraised value.

Your parcel's own appraisal and any exemptions drive the real bill. Multiply the appraisal by 25 percent, divide by 100 and apply your location's rate to estimate it.

When are Roane County property taxes due?

October 1 is the due date on the Assessor's calendar. Notices usually go out in late September, and payment is accepted until the end of February. Delinquency starts March 1.

Plenty of owners pay in winter, and that is permitted. Once a house is listed, though, an open current-year bill turns up in the title search and gets paid at closing. Paying in the fall takes one line off the settlement statement.

Payment can be made in three ways. Online carries a convenience fee that the county does not keep. United Community Bank in Kingston and SimplyBank in Rockwood and Harriman accept payments free. Partial payments are taken at the office if you come in person.

How assessments and appeals work

Every parcel is valued as of January 1, on a four-year reappraisal cycle whose latest round came in 2025. Between rounds a value changes only if the property itself does, so selling a house does not reset the number.

  • January 1: assessment date for ownership, assessments and tax maps
  • March 15: deadline to apply for greenbelt on land of 15 acres or more used for agriculture or forestry
  • May: assessment change notices go to owners whose appraisal changed
  • June 1: the County Board of Equalization begins hearing appeals
  • October 1: taxes are due to the Trustee

When a notice looks high, phone the Assessor at 865-376-4362 and ask which comparable sales back the figure. If the call settles nothing, carry that information to the Board of Equalization. The filing deadline moves from year to year, so ask the office for the current one.

What tax relief and greenbelt options exist?

Three tools are on offer, and each goes through a different counter.

  • State tax relief for homeowners 65 or older, homeowners who are 100 percent disabled, certain service-connected disabled veteran owners and spouses of a veteran killed in action. The Trustee handles the paperwork, the state decides eligibility, and the income limit changes each year.
  • The property tax freeze, adopted by the County Commission in 2007 under a state program. It is open to homeowners 65 or older under a state income limit, with no more than 5 acres, and the Trustee takes the annual application.
  • Greenbelt, filed with the Assessor by March 15, for farm or forest tracts of 15 acres or more.

Greenbelt carries a price on exit. When land stops qualifying, a roll-back charge equal to the taxes saved over the last three years comes due. A buyer or seller of a farm parcel should ask the Assessor whether greenbelt status is attached before a contract is signed.

What happens to delinquent taxes?

Delinquent bills stay in the Trustee's office for 18 months before they pass to the Clerk and Master. A Chancery Court suit follows in March of the next year, with filing fees added and monthly interest still running. Ask both offices which one holds your year. Once the suit is filed, you pay the Clerk and Master and not the Trustee, and partial payments for a tax year are refused.

You can stop a sale by paying everything owed before the sale begins. The Clerk and Master asks for the map, group and parcel number and takes a business or cashier's check, a call to 865-376-2487, or an in-person payment. Call for a total, because interest adds on every month.

The county holds a back tax sale once a year at the courthouse, and the next one is set for March 6, 2027. Property sells as is, bidders must be 18 or older and registered before the sale, and the court must confirm each sale. The usual redemption period is one year from the confirming order. For properties sold at the March 2027 sale where taxes are more than three years delinquent, a law that took effect July 1, 2026 cuts that to 90 days.

Selling a Roane County house with tax due

Request a payoff and settle it from the sale proceeds. While the bill is in the Trustee's hands, that office quotes the figure. After a lawsuit, the Clerk and Master does.

  • Ask which office holds each year, since the answer decides where the check goes.
  • Give the closing agent the map, group and parcel number from your tax bill.
  • If you owe more than one year, request a total as of your closing date.
  • A city lot in Harriman, Kingston, Rockwood, Oak Ridge or Oliver Springs can carry a city charge as well, and the Clerk and Master collects delinquent city taxes too.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as is can close on a short timeline when the payoff is clean. That helps when a tax sale date is approaching.

Roane County housing snapshot

The county spans 395 square miles. Kingston is the seat, and Oak Ridge is the biggest city. Harriman, Rockwood and Oliver Springs are the other incorporated places. The Census estimate is 57,395 people on July 1, 2025, up 7.2 percent from the 2020 base. There are 26,696 housing units and a 78.1 percent owner-occupancy rate. Median household income is $71,885 and median rent is $785. The county issued 380 building permits in 2025.

Frequently asked questions

When are Roane County property taxes due?

October 1 is the due date on the Assessor's calendar, and the tax is payable through the end of February. Unpaid bills become delinquent on March 1.

What is the 2026 Roane County property tax rate?

The county rate is $1.4523 per $100 of assessed value for city residents and $1.4987 outside the cities. City rates add to the county rate: Rockwood $0.6265, Harriman $0.7024, Kingston $0.8234, Oliver Springs $0.92 and Oak Ridge $1.3784.

Where can I pay Roane County property tax in person?

At the Trustee's office in the Courthouse, 200 E. Race Street, Suite 4, Kingston, or at United Community Bank in Kingston or SimplyBank in Rockwood and Harriman, where no fee is charged. Online payments carry a convenience fee.

When is the next Roane County tax sale?

The Clerk and Master lists the next Back Tax Sale for March 6, 2027. You can pay delinquent taxes up to the day of the sale, before it begins, to take a parcel off the list.

Can I freeze my Roane County property tax?

Possibly. Homeowners 65 or older with income under the state limit and no more than 5 acres can apply to the Trustee for the tax freeze each year. Call 865-376-4938 for the form and the current limit.

Robertson County offices that value and bill property

In Springfield, two elected offices divide the job. One, the Assessor of Property, decides what land and buildings are worth. The other, the County Trustee, sends out the bills and collects payment. The Register of Deeds files the deeds that tie the two together.

  • Assessor of Property: 521 S. Brown St., Springfield, 615-384-4311, weekday hours 8 to 4:30.
  • County Trustee: Room 161 of the Robertson County Office Building, 515 S. Brown St., 615-384-4238, Monday through Friday until 4:30 p.m.
  • Register of Deeds: same weekday schedule.

With so many parcels passing through the Trustee's hands, get any payoff figure in writing and do not rely on a phone estimate.

Robertson County housing and what it means for a sale

Robertson County sits on the Kentucky line and belongs to the Nashville metropolitan area. Mid 2025 estimates count 80,175 residents, which is 10.1 percent above the 2020 base of 72,809. The typical owned home is valued at $335,000 for 2020 to 2024, household income runs $83,047, and owners occupy 77.6 percent of homes. Median rent is $1,199 a month. Springfield is the county seat, and the county also includes Adams, Cedar Hill, Cross Plains, Greenbrier, Orlinda, Coopertown, Ridgetop and White House.

Tax calendar and late payment costs

You can pay from the first Monday of October through the last day of February. On March 1, and again at the start of each later month, state law piles on 1.5 percent interest.

Robertson County real property tax calendar

Where can I send a Robertson County tax payment?

Several routes work, including the counter, mail, web, phone and bank draft. The trustee takes partial payments and prepayments for as long as a bill stays in that office.

  • In person: Room 161 of the county office building during office hours, or the drop box by the sliding front door.
  • Drive thru: a kiosk lane at the office building.
  • Local banks: The Farmers Bank (all branches) and United Community Bank in Springfield, current year only and October through February, with the paper notice in hand.
  • Online or phone: tnproptax.com or 1-877-556-4079. The vendor charges 2.50 percent on cards or $1.25 on e-checks, plus $0.30 for phone payments, and the county keeps none of it.
  • Mail: the postmark date counts for interest.
  • Auto draft: monthly on the 10th, with the enrollment form received before the first of the prior month.

Most mortgage servicers send payment in December. Confirm it posted at tnproptax.com long before March 1.

Who owes the tax if a house sells mid-year?

The January 1 owner carries the liability, although a sales contract can move the cost to someone else. The trustee has no record of those contracts, so making sure the bill is paid remains your responsibility.

Timing adds a wrinkle. The Assessor receives a copy of every recorded deed the next day, but about 90 days go by before the parcel shows the buyer's name. The notice follows whatever name was on file January 1, so the closing papers should settle who pays. Mortgage companies do not receive tax notices by mail.

Before closing, ask the trustee for a current balance on every parcel you own. Deeds are indexed under different spellings of a name, so a search by name alone can miss one.

How to dispute a Robertson County assessment

A dispute climbs three rungs: the Assessor's office, the local equalization board, then the state board. County boards typically open June 1 and sit until their caseload is cleared.

If the county board's answer disappoints you, you have until August 1 of that tax year, or 45 days after the notice date if that is later, to file at the state level (T.C.A. 67-5-1412(e)). Processing cost is capped at $10 per filing. Values are fixed as of January 1, so events after that date generally do not affect the value, and recent comparable sales are the strongest evidence of what a house is worth.

Search by owner name, address or parcel number on the state-run Tennessee Property Data site, which the Assessor links to, and compare the record with the real house before you pick up the phone.

Relief and special programs from the Trustee

The Trustee runs three programs for eligible owners: a Tax Relief Program, a Tax Freeze Program and a Wheel Tax Rebate. Call 615-384-4238 for current requirements and application timing.

Farmland owners should also know about greenbelt. The Assessor mails greenbelt applications within 90 days of a processed deed. If land leaves agricultural, forest or open space use, rollback taxes apply: the difference between use value and market value for the preceding three years for farm and forest land, or five years for open space. They are not a penalty, and they become delinquent March 15 of the following year (T.C.A. 67-5-1008(d)). Anyone selling acreage should ask the Assessor whether a change of use is coming.

Selling a Robertson County house with tax still due

Yes. The balance simply becomes part of the sale. Buyers, lenders and title companies all want the exact figure, so ask the trustee to put it in writing.

Where the bill sits depends on its age. A real property bill under one year delinquent stays with the trustee, who accepts partial payments. After it is turned over, you pay through Robertson County Chancery Court at 615-384-5650, and added costs apply. Delinquent personal property tax for 2015 through 2024 can be paid through American Financial Credit Services at 888-317-2327 extension 3.

  1. Find out from the trustee what stage each year's bill has reached.
  2. Get the payoff in writing for your expected closing date.
  3. Have the settlement statement list the trustee payoff on its own line.

A cash purchase can proceed even with tax outstanding, though weigh the payoff against the price on the table.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Robertson County property tax deadline?

The last day of February ends the interest-free period, and 1.5 percent interest starts March 1.

Where do I pay property tax in Robertson County?

Room 161 of the county office building, 515 S. Brown St. in Springfield, takes payments, as do the drop box, the drive thru, two named local banks, tnproptax.com and the mail.

How long does a deed take to show up with the Robertson County Assessor?

About 90 days. The Assessor gets a copy the day after recording, then moves the parcel into the new owner's name. The tax bill goes to the January 1 owner until the next year.

Can I appeal my Robertson County assessment after the county board meets?

Yes. The State Board of Equalization takes appeals filed by August 1 or within 45 days of the county board's notice, whichever comes later. Begin with the Assessor at 615-384-4311.

Does Robertson County have a property tax relief program for seniors?

The Trustee runs a Tax Relief Program and a Tax Freeze Program. Call 615-384-4238 for eligibility rules and application timing, because the trustee sets the current requirements.

Who bills and collects

Three separate offices touch a Tipton County tax bill. The Assessor values every parcel. The county commission and each city council set rates. The Trustee mails the bills and takes the money. The Assessor's office does not set the rate, send bills or collect taxes.

The Trustee works from 1 Pleasant Avenue, Room 203, in Covington (mailing address PO Box 487, Covington, TN 38019), phone 901-476-0211, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00. During tax season a second counter opens at Munford City Hall, 1397 Munford Avenue, every Wednesday from the first Wednesday in October through February 24, 2027, with a few holiday dates skipped. Questions about value or a mailing address go to the Assessor at 901-476-0213.

City tax is separate. City taxes are not collected at the county counter, so use the municipal offices:

  • Covington, 200 W Washington Avenue, 901-476-9613
  • Atoka, 334 Atoka-Munford Avenue, 901-837-5300
  • Brighton, 1270 Old Highway 51 S, 901-476-8661
  • Mason, 12157 Main Street, 901-294-3525
  • Munford, 1397 Munford Avenue, 901-837-0171

Covington sets its own due date at October 1 and its delinquency date at March 1, refuses partial payments, and charges a city rate of $1.0128 for each $100 of assessed value. A Covington house therefore carries a county bill and a city bill.

Market context

Tipton County lies on the western edge of Tennessee along the Mississippi River, with Covington as the county seat, and it belongs to the Memphis metro area. U.S. Highway 51 runs north to south through Covington. The county sits on the southeastern edge of the New Madrid Seismic Zone, an area of high earthquake risk, which is a fair question to raise with an insurer. Covington's South Main Historic District keeps about 50 homes from the late 1800s and early 1900s, and the district is federally registered.

Population was 62,287 in July 2025, up 2.2% since April 2020. There are 25,033 housing units, and 76.3% of occupied ones are owned by their residents. A typical owned home is worth $240,600, and typical rent is $1,013. Only 139 building permits were issued in 2025, so new construction competes lightly with resale homes.

How the bill is figured

The Assessor sets an appraised value, the state assessment ratio turns that into assessed value, and the rate is applied per $100. The ratios are residential 25 percent, farm 25 percent, commercial and industrial 40 percent, personal property 30 percent, and public utility 55 percent. The 2026 county rate is $1.3417 per $100, down from $1.5217 in 2025. The rate has fallen steadily in the history the Trustee posts:

Tipton County is on a six-year reappraisal cycle: five years of on-site review of every parcel, then a revaluation in the sixth year. Ask the Assessor which year of the cycle the county is in, since a revaluation year is when the value of a house tends to move most.

Due dates, interest and ways to pay

Billing opens on the first Monday in October, and the interest-free period runs through the last day of February. On March 1 the account is delinquent. The Trustee then adds 1.5 percent on the first of each month and rounds to the nearest dollar. The schedule reads 1.5 percent in March, 3.0 in April and 4.5 in May, reaching 18.0 percent in February of the following year and 19.5 in March.

The notice leaves the office in the first week of October, addressed to the January 1 owner. The Trustee takes payment in these ways:

  • At the Covington counter, or at the Wednesday Munford counter during the season
  • Online through the Trustee's payment portal, where the vendor adds 2.5 percent on a card or $1.25 on an online check
  • By phone at 1-855-548-3603, with a $0.30 processing fee on top of the vendor charges
  • By bank draft, either in one annual payment, in four payments from November to February, or monthly, arranged at 901-476-0211

Partial payments are welcome, but interest is added to whatever remains after February 28. A refund is only issued on a parcel that another agency, such as a lender, has already paid. No other reason qualifies.

How to dispute your value

A Tipton County owner who thinks the roll overstates a house has two steps. First comes the local County Board of Equalization. The Assessor posts the roll for public viewing in May and mails notices on parcels whose value moved, and the board's ruling closes out the roll for that year. Second comes the state equalization board, which takes a filing up to August 1, or 45 days after the local notice went out, whichever is later. Read the date printed on your notice.

Facts and numbers carry a hearing. The state's guidance names three kinds of proof:

  • Recent sales of look-alike homes nearby, with adjustments for size, age and condition
  • A written appraisal from a professional who is ready to testify
  • Your own figure for the value, backed by reasons

Pay the part of the tax you do not dispute before March 1, along with any older delinquent tax. The State Board's phone line is 615-401-7883.

Property tax relief

The state reimburses part or all of the tax for low-income elderly and disabled homeowners, disabled former service members, and their widowed spouses. The program dates to 1973. The Trustee's 2026 income cap is $38,470 from every source, for the applicant, spouse and any other owner, measured on 2025 income. Because it is a reimbursement and not an exemption, the bill is paid first.

Paperwork differs by group. Elderly applicants bring 2025 income proof and a Medicare or Social Security card. Disabled applicants bring proof of age plus a benefits letter when the payer is not Social Security. Disabled former service members sign an F-16 and show ID. Mobile home owners add a title, bill of sale or affidavit of affixation. The office begins the 2026 process in October, so call 901-476-0211 to book.

Selling with taxes owed

The January 1 owner is on the roll, so a house sold in the fall still carries a bill in the seller's name. At closing the title company normally splits the year, and the buyer takes over from there. If you owe tax, ask the Trustee for the exact payoff, including any interest, before setting a closing date. Interest climbs each month after February, so a quick closing, including a cash sale that skips lender delays, limits how much extra you pay.

Gather these before you call: the parcel number, the name on the notice, and the date you hope to close. If the house is inside Covington, Atoka, Brighton, Mason or Munford, ask that city's office for a separate figure, because the Trustee does not collect city tax.

Frequently asked questions

What rate applies to a Tipton County house in 2026?

The 2026 county rate is $1.3417 for each $100 of assessed value, lower than the $1.5217 charged in 2025. City tax is billed separately, and Covington lists $1.0128 per $100.

How long can I wait to pay Tipton County tax before interest begins?

The last interest-free day is February 28. Billing opens on the first Monday in October, and each month after that date adds 1.5 percent.

Where can I hand over a Tipton County tax payment?

Pay at the Trustee's office at 1 Pleasant Avenue, Room 203, in Covington, or on Wednesdays at Munford City Hall during tax season. Online, phone and bank draft payments are also offered.

Can I get a refund of Tipton County property tax?

Only on a parcel that another agency has already paid, such as a lender. Refunds are not issued for any other reason.

Which number reaches the Tipton County Assessor?

The Assessor's line is 901-476-0213. That office can talk through a value and explain how to get on the county board's schedule.

Selling in Greene County: local context

Greene County stretches along Tennessee's eastern border. Greeneville is the seat and the largest town, and Tusculum is the county's one city, with Baileyton, Greeneville and Mosheim as towns. Population reached 73,831 by mid-2025, a 5.2 percent gain on the April 2020 count. Of 33,581 housing units, owners hold 77.1 percent. The usual owner-occupied value is $207,500, and owners pay $1,150 a month with a mortgage or $361 without. Builders took out 276 permits in 2025.

School district boundaries matter to buyers. Greeneville City Schools covers addresses inside the Greeneville limits, and Greene County Schools serves everything outside them. Know which one your street falls in before you list.

Who handles property tax in Greene County

Work is split three ways. Voters elect the assessor, who values every parcel, and the trustee, who mails bills and deposits payments. The county commission picks the rate. The trustee's page is clear that the trustee has no say in how large a bill is.

The trustee is at the Greene County Government Administration Center, 401 Takoma Avenue, Suite 104, Greeneville, TN 37743, phone 423-798-1705, open Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The Assessor of Property is down the hall at Suite 106, phone 423-798-1738.

The Town of Greeneville taxes property as well, and its Recorder's Office takes those payments. A home inside town limits therefore produces a county bill and a town bill. For addresses in Mosheim, Baileyton or Tusculum, ask who collects the municipal share. Depending on the city, that may be its treasurer, its recorder or the county trustee.

How the bill is figured

The formula is assessed value times the rate, divided by $100. Houses and farmland are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, while commercial and industrial property is assessed at 40 percent. Ask the trustee for the rate in force, because the commission and the town set theirs on separate schedules.

The trustee also explains where the money goes. Property tax is the largest local source for the general fund, with the wheel tax second. The school fund leans mostly on state education dollars, followed by property tax and local sales tax.

To estimate your own bill, take the appraised value from your notice, apply the 25 percent ratio, divide by 100 and multiply by the combined rate. If the house sits inside Greeneville, remember to add the town's share, which is billed and collected separately.

Due dates and how to pay

The county begins taking payments the first Monday of October, with no interest until the end of February. Bills turn delinquent on March 1.

A notice goes out by mail even though state law does not demand one. Interest runs whether or not it reaches you. Call 423-798-1705 if yours never came, and call the assessor at 423-798-1738 to correct the address on file.

Greene County property tax calendar
DateWhat happens

First Monday of OctoberCounty payments accepted
End of FebruaryLast day free of interest
March 1Bill is delinquent
June 1County equalization board opens
August 1Usual state appeal cutoff

The trustee accepts payment these ways:

  • In person at Suite 104, using cash, a check, a money order or a debit or credit card
  • By mail, with the stub enclosed and the receipt number noted on the check; a postmark is accepted
  • By phone at 1-833-591-7184 or online at tnproptax.com
  • Through the deposit slot just inside the Administration Center's main entrance

A vendor charges 2.5 percent on cards and $1.25 on online ACH payments. The county keeps none of it.

How to contest a Greene County value

Your first stop is the county equalization board, which starts hearing cases on June 1 each year. Skip it and the value generally stands. The assessor's office schedules you.

Losing locally does not end the matter. The State Board of Equalization takes the next appeal, filed by August 1 of that tax year or within 45 days of the county board's mailed decision, whichever date is later. A state judge holds a hearing and rules in writing within 90 days. You carry the burden of showing the right number. Reach the state board at 615-401-7883.

Evidence that persuades:

  • Closed sales of similar houses, with allowances for size, age, condition and location
  • An appraiser's report, with the appraiser ready to appear
  • A concrete dollar value you propose, since calling the house overvalued rarely works

While the case runs, pay the undisputed share of the bill by the delinquency date and settle any prior-year balances, or the case may be stalled or thrown out.

Tax relief for Greene County homeowners

Tennessee runs a refund-style relief program for low-income seniors, disabled owners, disabled military service members and certain surviving spouses. For 2026 an elderly or disabled applicant's 2025 income cannot exceed $38,470, and the refund is worked out on no more than $33,600 of market value. For disabled military service members the cap on value is $175,000. You must own and live in the house, and seniors need to reach 65 by December 31, 2026.

Because relief reimburses tax already paid, you settle the bill first. The trustee takes applications from the first Monday of October through March and wants a phone call beforehand to list the documents. The state brochure ties the final date to 35 days past delinquency, so confirm the exact day with the office.

A separate local-option freeze exists for owners 65 and up, but only in counties that adopted it. Greene is not among the 28 adopting counties on the state list, so ask the trustee whether that has changed.

What happens to the bill when your house sells

At closing the buyer and seller usually share the year's tax by proration. Trustee staff stay out of it. Your closing agent calculates the split and lists it on the settlement statement.

Owe back tax? Ask the trustee for a payoff figure now, as interest keeps adding up. A seller with an inherited house, an empty house or a lot of repairs can have the title company settle the balance from sale proceeds. Recording the deed and paying the state's $0.37 per $100 transfer tax both happen at the register of deeds.

Before listing, collect three items: the payoff or current balance from the trustee, the parcel's record from the assessor, and your last bill. They tell a buyer that no tax surprise is waiting.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Greene County property tax rate?

Call the trustee at 423-798-1705 for the current figure, since the county commission and the Town of Greeneville each set a rate. The formula is assessed value times rate over 100, and homes are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value.

When do Greene County property taxes go delinquent?

March 1. You can start paying the first Monday of October, interest-free until February ends. Interest then accrues until the balance is cleared.

Who should I contact about my Greene County property value?

The Assessor of Property at 423-798-1738, 401 Takoma Avenue, Suite 106, Greeneville. That office answers value questions, updates mailing addresses and starts the process toward the county equalization board.

Can seniors in Greene County get a tax break?

Yes, through the state relief program if 2025 income was $38,470 or less and the applicant owns and lives in the home. The trustee takes applications. The local freeze exists only where a county adopted it, and Greene is not on the state list.

Who pays the property tax at a Greene County closing?

Both sides, by proration. The trustee's office does not split the bill. Your title company or closing agent does it and shows the result on the settlement statement.

Phone the Assessor of Property at 423-542-1801, or try the real estate assessment data link on the county assessor page. Homes are assessed at 25 percent of the appraised figure.

The Trustee handles delinquent questions at 423-542-1811. Taxes more than 13 months past due go through the Clerk and Master at 423-542-1812, which also runs tax sales.

Yes. Relief is a state reimbursement, not an exemption. You receive the bill, pay it, and the state repays all or part of the taxes paid.

A residential owner's file should hold comparable sales from one or two years before the tax year, a recent paid appraisal, and exterior and interior photos. Pack a driver's license, Medicare card and Social Security card, together with income documents for yourself, your spouse and any other owner. For a mobile home, add a title copy or bill of sale. Probably the seller's. The January 1 owner stays on record for the whole year, and the closing attorney divides the cost between buyer and seller.

How long does the Board of Equalization meet?

Around two weeks, early in June, with weekday hearings and appointments taken in late May. Call (731) 423-6063 to confirm this year's schedule.

Who to call about property tax

The Trustee sends bills; the Assessor of Property answers questions about value. The Trustee is based at the courthouse in Athens, and the County Commission picks the rate.

  • Trustee: McMinn County Courthouse, 6 East Madison Avenue, Athens, TN 37303. Phone (423) 745-1291, fax (423) 744-1603.
  • Hours: Monday to Friday, 8:00 to 4:00, with extra Saturday mornings in February, 8:30 to noon.
  • Assessor of Property: appraises and classifies every parcel, checks sales, and takes reappraisal questions.

The Trustee's page describes three jobs for the office: collecting county property tax, keeping the county's accounts, and investing idle funds. The state tax relief program also runs through it. October mailings go to the January 1 owner, who is responsible for keeping the Assessor's mailing address up to date.

McMinn County at a glance

The county seat, Athens, is also the largest city. Etowah, Niota and Sweetwater are cities as well, with Calhoun, Englewood and Riceville rounding out the list. On July 1, 2025 the county had 57,404 residents, 7.8% more than in April 2020, and 24,424 housing units, of which 75.8% are lived in by their owners. Typical owner-occupied value is $211,800, typical rent is $803, and the median household earns $61,470. Builders pulled 125 permits in 2025.

School lines matter to buyers. McMinn County Schools runs most of the public schools, including McMinn County High and McMinn Central High. Athens City Schools and the Etowah School District cover grades K to 8 in their own areas, with the county high schools taking those students after eighth grade. Tennessee Wesleyan University is in Athens.

Tax rate for 2026 to 2027

For the fiscal year starting July 1, 2026, the combined county rate is $1.0823 on each $100 of assessed value. Resolution 26-036, passed by the County Commission on June 15, 2026, set it, and the Trustee may round statements to a whole dollar. State classes drive assessment: farm and residential 25 percent, personal property 30 percent, industrial and commercial 40 percent, public utilities 55 percent.

Six funds share the levy, three of them school funds for McMinn, Athens and Etowah.

McMinn County levy by fund, per $100 of assessed value

General Fund$0.4828

Total$1.0823

Cities can add their own tax to the county figure, so ask whether yours does. Rates are set each summer for the fiscal year beginning July 1, which means the number on a bill mailed in October reflects that June vote. If you are comparing years, remember that the assessed value, not the rate alone, drives the total.

Due dates and penalties

Pay anytime from October 1 through the last day of February with no penalty. From March 1 the Trustee charges penalty and interest of 1.5 percent a month on what is unpaid.

You may mail payment; the postmark counts, and a receipt comes back the same way. A delinquent tax lien stays on the parcel through any change of owner, so buyers should run a title check. Old taxes must be paid before new ones, so a payment meant for this year first goes against any prior-year balance.

The office also opens on Saturday mornings in February. For payment methods beyond mail and in-person, call (423) 745-1291.

Disputing a value

Talk to the Assessor of Property first, then go to the local equalization board. Under state law the county board hears a dispute before anyone else, and skipping it generally makes the value final. The Comptroller's appeals guide describes the board as five or more people who hear complaints and can change assessments.

  • County board: file by the date the Assessor gives you for this year's session.
  • State Board of Equalization: file by August 1 or on the 45th day after the county board mailed notice, whichever comes later.
  • Hearing: an administrative judge, who must put the decision in writing within 90 days.
  • Chancery court: petition within 60 days of the state board's final order.

One more rule for business owners: when a business fails to file a personal property schedule, the county forces an assessment, and only an appeal to the local board before that year's deadline can undo it. The schedule itself is due before March 1.

Homeowners should keep any appeal paperwork together: the Assessor's notice, your comparable sales, photos and the date you filed. If you miss a deadline, ask the Assessor or Trustee what options remain before assuming the value is final.

Tax relief

A state-funded program, run through the Trustee, helps elderly owners, disabled owners and disabled-veteran owners. Qualifying applicants have part of the home's tax paid by the State of Tennessee. File no later than 35 days after the February 28 payment deadline, which means early April. A veteran with a 100 percent rating may have other programs open. Bring proof of age, disability or rating, and income records when you apply, and ask the Trustee which documents it needs for your category before you go.

Income limits and credit amounts are set by the state each year, so call (423) 745-1291 for this year's figures before you apply. Relief repays part of a bill you have paid, so the bill itself still arrives.

Selling a McMinn County house with tax owed

A buyer's title search will turn up every unpaid year, because past-due tax stays attached to the house. It binds the property no matter who owns it, so a seller who is behind should expect the title company to insist on payoff at closing.

Before accepting an offer, get each year's amount from the Trustee, interest included. For an inherited house, one behind on payments or one needing repairs, the tax balance is simply another figure the title company takes from proceeds, and learning it early protects your closing date. Ask, too, whether a delinquent balance has accrued monthly interest since March 1, because the amount changes each month until paid.

A seller's to-do list: call (423) 745-1291 for the balance on each year, have the Assessor correct a wrong owner name or mailing address, pass the numbers to the title company, and look for the payoff on the settlement statement. Cash sales on short timelines follow the same list, just faster, and a clear payoff letter speeds them further. Do the calls early in the week, because the courthouse closes at four and the Saturday hours apply only in February, and write down the name of whoever gives you each figure.

Frequently asked questions

What is the current McMinn County property tax rate?

$1.0823 per $100 of assessed value covers the fiscal year that began July 1, 2026, and the County Commission set it on June 15, 2026. Homes are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value.

When does McMinn County charge interest on late taxes?

From March 1 on, at 1.5 percent a month. You can pay penalty-free from October 1 until the last day of February.

Can I mail my McMinn County property tax?

Yes. The postmark date decides whether you were on time, and the Trustee mails back a receipt.

Which school systems affect a McMinn County tax bill?

Three funds on the levy support schools: McMinn, Athens and Etowah. Athens City Schools and the Etowah School District serve grades K to 8 in their areas, while McMinn County Schools covers most of the rest.

Do I need to pay old McMinn County taxes before this year's?

Yes, past-due taxes come first, and any such balance stays with the parcel whoever owns it.
